verses.translation: And after{H310} this I saw{H7200} four{H702} messengers{H4397} standing{H5975} at the four{H702} corners{H6438} of the earth{H776}, and holding back{H662} the four{H702} winds{H7307} of the earth{H776}, so that there would be no wind{H7307} upon the earth{H776} or upon the waters{H4325} or upon any tree{H6086}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִתְאַפְּקִים (mit'apqim, H662 — hitpael of אפק, 'restraining/holding back'). The hitpael implies the messengers are straining to restrain forces that resist them — holding themselves firm against the winds' pressure. Greek κρατοῦντας ('holding/seizing') is simple active. A back-translator from Greek would use מַחֲזִיקִים (machzikim — 'holding') or אוֹחֲזִים (ochazim — 'grasping'), not the reflexive-intensive hitpael form. Compare Gen 43:31 and 45:1 where Joseph 'restrained himself' (וַיִּתְאַפַּק) — the same root conveying forceful self-control.

Uses הַמַּיִם (ha-mayim — 'the waters', H4325) in v1 but הַיָּם (ha-yam — 'the sea', H3220) in vv2-3. Greek uses θάλασσα ('sea') in all three verses. The Hebrew author DISTINGUISHES: the wind affects all 'waters' (rivers, lakes, seas), but the messengers' commission to 'harm' targets specifically 'the sea.' A back-translator seeing θάλασσα three times in Greek would use יָם three times. The Hebrew variation is deliberate and meaningful.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the waters' (הַמַּיִם). Greek: 'the sea' (τῆς θαλάσσης). Hebrew is broader — all water surfaces.
translation_notes: 'Holding back' for mit'apqim — the hitpael of אפק conveys forceful restraint against resistance, not merely passive holding.
שׁוּם (shum — 'any') is a post-biblical Hebrew word, characteristic of Mishnaic usage.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} another{H312} messenger{H4397} who came{H935} from the rising{H4217} of the sun{H8121}, and he had the seal{H2368} from the living{H2416} and enduring El{H410}; and he cried out{H6817} with a great{H1419} voice{H6963} to the four{H702} messengers{H4397} who were given{H5414} to harm the earth{H776} and the sea{H3220}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חוֹתָם (chotam, H2368 — 'seal/signet ring') — the specific OT word for a personal signet used for authentication and identity. Judah's chotam (Gen 38:18), the priestly breastplate engravings 'like the engravings of a chotam' (Ex 28:11,21), and Haggai 2:23 where YHWH makes Zerubbabel 'like a chotam.' Greek σφραγῖδα is a generic 'seal.' The Hebrew word carries the weight of personal identity and covenant authorization.

Uses the paired expression חַי וְקִיֵּים (chai v'qayyem — 'living and enduring'). This matches Daniel 6:27 (Aramaic: חַי וְקַיָּם) where Daniel declares God is 'the living and enduring God.' Greek ζῶντος has only 'living' — omitting the distinctly Aramaic/Daniel term קַיָּם entirely. A back-translator from Greek, seeing only ζῶντος, would write חַי alone, never independently adding the Daniel-specific formula.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'living and enduring' (חַי וְקִיֵּים — paired expression). Greek: 'living' (ζῶντος) only. The Aramaic pair is reduced to a single adjective.
translation_notes: 'From the rising of the sun' (מִמִּזְרַח הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ) is a standard OT phrase for 'from the east' (Deut 4:41, Josh 1:15, Mal 1:11). It is more vivid than a simple directional word.
קִיֵּים (qayyem — 'enduring/established') is a post-biblical/Aramaic form from the root קום. No standard Strong's number.
לְהַזִּיק (lehazziq — 'to harm/damage') is a Mishnaic Hebrew causative form, characteristic of post-biblical Hebrew.
textual_notes: Daniel 6:27 (Aramaic): 'He is the living God and enduring forever' (אֱלָהָא חַיָּא וְקַיָּם לְעָלְמִין). The Hebrew Revelation preserves this Danielic divine description.

verses.translation: And he said{H559}: Do not{H408} harm the earth{H776} or the sea{H3220} or the tree{H6086}, until{H5704} I place{H5414} a mark{H8420} upon the foreheads{H4696} of the servants{H5650} of YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תָּו (tav, H8420 — 'a mark/sign') — the specific word from Ezekiel 9:4 where YHWH commands: 'Pass through Jerusalem and put a תָּו upon the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations.' The Hebrew תָּו is the name of the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which in ancient paleo-Hebrew script was written as a cross-mark (×/+). Greek σφραγίσωμεν ('we shall seal') uses a generic sealing verb. A back-translator from Greek would write נַחְתֹּם (nachtom — 'we shall seal') from חתם (H2856), NEVER the Ezekiel-specific תָּו. The Hebrew author sees this scene as the fulfillment of Ezekiel 9.

Uses first person SINGULAR אֶתֵּן (eten — 'I shall place', H5414). Greek has first person PLURAL σφραγίσωμεν ('we shall seal'). The Hebrew presents the messenger acting with sole authority; the Greek implies collective action. A back-translator from the Greek plural would write נחתום ('we shall seal'), not the singular 'I shall place.'

Uses עַבְדֵי יַהְוֶה (avdei YHWH — 'servants of YHWH') with the Tetragrammaton. Greek: τοὺς δούλους τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν ('the servants of our God'). A back-translator from Greek would write עַבְדֵי אֱלֹהֵינוּ ('servants of our Elohim'), not the covenant name YHWH.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: singular 'the tree' (לָעֵץ). Greek: plural 'the trees' (τὰ δένδρα).
Hebrew: 'I shall place a mark' (first singular, action = placing a tav). Greek: 'we shall seal' (first plural, action = sealing). Different person, different verb, different concept.
Hebrew: 'servants of YHWH' (Tetragrammaton). Greek: 'servants of our God' (τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν).
translation_notes: 'Mark' for tav — preserving the Ezekiel 9:4 connection. The tav-mark is not a generic seal but a specific prophetic sign.

The Hebrew distinguishes three concepts across vv2-4: the חוֹתָם (chotam — the seal instrument, v2), the תָּו (tav — the mark placed, v3), and the verb חתם (chatam — the action of sealing, v4). Greek σφραγίς/σφραγίζω collapses all three into one concept.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 9:4,6 — 'Go through the city, through Jerusalem, and put a mark (תָּו) upon the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations... but touch no one upon whom is the mark.' The tav-mark is explicitly a sign of protection from judgment, exactly as in this context.

verses.translation: And I heard{H8085} the number{H4557} of those who were sealed{H2856}: a hundred{H3967} and forty{H705}-four{H702} thousands{H505}, sealed{H2856} from the clans{H4940} of the sons{H1121} of Yisrael{H3478}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מִשְׁפְּחוֹת (mishpechot — 'clans/families', H4940) — the specific Israelite kinship unit BELOW the שֵׁבֶט (tribe) in the biblical hierarchy: tribe → clan → household (see Josh 7:14-18, Num 1:2). Greek ἐκ πάσης φυλῆς ('from every tribe') uses the generic 'tribe' and adds 'every' (πάσης) which is absent from Hebrew. A back-translator from Greek φυλή would use שֵׁבֶט (shevet — 'tribe'), not the more specific mishpachah. The Hebrew author preserves the nuanced Israelite social structure: the sealing penetrates to the clan level within each tribe.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the clans' (מִמִּשְׁפְּחוֹת — without 'every'). Greek: 'from every tribe' (ἐκ πάσης φυλῆς — adds 'every' and uses 'tribe' not 'clan').
translation_notes: 'Clans' for mishpechot preserves the Hebrew social hierarchy. The next four verses (5-8) then enumerate by שֵׁבֶט (tribe), showing the Hebrew author uses both terms precisely: sealed at the clan level, listed by tribal identity.
אֵילּוּ (eilu — 'those') is a distinctly post-biblical/Mishnaic Hebrew demonstrative pronoun.
textual_notes: The Hebrew number expression 'a hundred and four and forty thousands' (מֵאָה וְאַרְבַּע וְאַרְבָּעִים אֲלָפִים) = 144,000, following standard Hebrew number order.

verses.translation: From the tribe{H7626} of Yehudah{H3063} twelve{H8147}{H6240} thousand{H505}; from the tribe{H7626} of Re'uven{H7205} twelve{H8147}{H6240} thousand{H505}; and from the tribe{H7626} of Gad{H1410} twelve{H8147}{H6240} thousand{H505}.

one_way_hebrew: Verse 4 uses מִשְׁפְּחוֹת (mishpechot — 'clans') but the enumeration in vv5-8 switches to שֵׁבֶט (shevet — 'tribe'). The Hebrew preserves a distinction between the kinship level of the sealing (clan) and the identity marker of the listing (tribe). Greek uses φυλή ('tribe') throughout, collapsing this distinction.
translation_notes: יְהוּדָא (Yehuda) is spelled with final aleph (א) instead of the standard Hebrew final he (ה) in יְהוּדָה. This Aramaic-influenced spelling appears in Ezra's Aramaic sections (Ezra 5:1,8). This spelling is characteristic of Hebrew/Aramaic manuscript tradition, not a feature a Greek back-translator would introduce.
textual_notes: Dan is absent from this twelve-tribe list; Levi (normally excluded from tribal land allotments) is included. Joseph replaces his son Ephraim. The list begins with Judah (the royal/messianic tribe) rather than Reuben (the firstborn). These rearrangements reflect deliberate theological choices rooted in Hebrew tribal traditions.

verses.translation: From the tribe{H7626} of Asher{H836} twelve{H8147}{H6240} thousand{H505}; from the tribe{H7626} of Naftali{H5321} twelve{H8147}{H6240} thousand{H505}; from the tribe{H7626} of Menasheh{H4519} twelve{H8147}{H6240} thousand{H505}.

From the tribe{H7626} of Shim'on{H8095} twelve{H8147}{H6240} thousand{H505}; from the tribe{H7626} of Levi{H3878} twelve{H8147}{H6240} thousand{H505}; and from the tribe{H7626} of Yissakhar{H3485} twelve{H8147}{H6240} thousand{H505}.

translation_notes: Levi's inclusion is notable — Levi is normally excluded from tribal land allotments (Num 18:20-24, Deut 10:9) because 'YHWH is their inheritance.' The inclusion of Levi in this sealing list suggests a priestly identity for the entire sealed community.

verses.translation: From the tribe{H7626} of Zevulun{H2074} twelve{H8147}{H6240} thousand{H505}; and from the tribe{H7626} of Yosef{H3130} twelve{H8147}{H6240} thousand{H505}; and from the tribe{H7626} of Binyamin{H1144} twelve{H8147}{H6240} thousand{H505}.

translation_notes: יוֹסֵף (Yosef) appears rather than his son אֶפְרַיִם (Ephraim). Since Menasheh (Joseph's other son) is listed separately in v6, Joseph here effectively stands in for Ephraim. This preserves the patriarchal name rather than the tribal subdivision.

verses.translation: And after this I saw{H7200} a great{H1419} fellowship that no one could{H3201} count{H5608}, from all{H3605} the peoples{H5971}, standing{H5975} before{H6440} the throne{H3678} and before the lamb{H7716}; and wearing{H3847} white{H3836} garments{H4403}, and in their hands{H3027} branches{H6057}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חַבְרוּתָה (chavruta — 'fellowship/company') — a distinctly Aramaic/Mishnaic term for an intimate communal group, later the standard word for a Torah study partnership in rabbinic literature. Greek ὄχλος πολύς ('a great crowd') describes an anonymous mass. A back-translator from Greek would use הָמוֹן (hamon — 'multitude') or קָהָל (qahal — 'assembly'), never the Aramaic-flavored chavruta. The Hebrew envisions this innumerable company as a fellowship, not a crowd.

CRITICAL: Uses עֲנָפִים (anafim — 'branches', H6057) — the GENERIC word for branches of any tree. Greek φοίνικες (phoinikes) specifically means 'palm branches.' A back-translator from Greek would use תְּמָרִים (temarim — 'palms') or כַּפּוֹת תְּמָרִים (kappot temarim — 'palm fronds', as in Lev 23:40). The Hebrew author uses the general word, evoking the Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles) lulav bundle which includes palm, willow, and myrtle branches (Lev 23:40). The Greek translator narrowed this to palms alone.

Hebrew: מִכָּל הָעַמִּים (mikol ha-amim — 'from all the peoples', one collective term). Greek: ἐκ παντὸς ἔθνους καὶ φυλῶν καὶ λαῶν καὶ γλωσσῶν ('from every nation and tribes and peoples and tongues' — fourfold list). A back-translator from Greek would reproduce the fourfold list. The Hebrew uses a single comprehensive term, the standard OT expression for gentile nations (Deut 7:7, 14:2).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a great fellowship' (חַבְרוּתָה גְּדוֹלָה). Greek: 'a great crowd' (ὄχλος πολύς). Different social concept.
Hebrew: 'from all the peoples' (one term). Greek: 'from every nation and tribes and peoples and tongues' (fourfold list). Greek adds 'tribes' and 'tongues' absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'branches' (עֲנָפִים — generic). Greek: 'palm branches' (φοίνικες — specific).
translation_notes: 'Fellowship' for chavruta — this Aramaic term carries connotations of intimate association absent from 'crowd.'

'Branches' for anafim is deliberately generic. In the Sukkot context (Lev 23:40), the commanded set includes 'fruit of goodly trees, branches of palm trees (כַּפֹּת תְּמָרִים), boughs of thick trees (עֲנַף עֵץ עָבוֹת), and willows of the brook.' The word עֲנָף itself appears in the Sukkot passage for the thick-tree boughs.
textual_notes: The Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles) imagery is unmistakable: a multitude holding branches before YHWH's throne, crying out declarations of salvation. During Sukkot, worshippers wave the lulav bundle and cry הוֹשַׁעְנָא (hoshana — 'save now!'). Zechariah 14:16 prophesies that in the age to come, all nations will go up to Jerusalem to celebrate Sukkot. This scene appears to be its fulfillment.

verses.translation: And crying out{H6817} with a great{H1419} voice{H6963} and saying{H559}: To YHWH{H3068} belongs the deliverance{H3444}, and to the lamb{H7716}!

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: לְיַהְוֶה הַיְשׁוּעָה (la-YHWH hayeshu'ah — 'To YHWH belongs the deliverance') is a DIRECT QUOTE from Psalm 3:9 [8]: לַיהוָה הַיְשׁוּעָה ('To YHWH belongs the salvation'). The Hebrew preserves this concise Psalm declaration and extends it: 'and to the lamb.' Greek expands this to Ἡ σωτηρία τῷ θεῷ ἡμῶν τῷ καθημένῳ ἐπὶ τοῦ θρόνου, καὶ τῷ ἀρνίῳ ('Salvation to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb'). A back-translator from the expanded Greek would write הַיְשׁוּעָה לֵאלֹהֵינוּ הַיֹּשֵׁב עַל הַכִּסֵּא, not the compact Psalm 3 quote. The Hebrew is shorter, more elegant, and scripturally rooted; the Greek is a theological expansion.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'To YHWH the deliverance, and to the lamb' (7 words, Psalm quotation). Greek: 'Salvation to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb' (expanded with throne description). The Hebrew is a concise Psalm quote; the Greek is a descriptive expansion.
Hebrew uses the Tetragrammaton (יַהְוֶה). Greek has 'our God' (τῷ θεῷ ἡμῶν).
translation_notes: 'Deliverance' for yeshu'ah (H3444) — the word contains the root of the name Yeshua (ישוע). The Hebrew naturally carries this wordplay; the Greek σωτηρία does not.
The cry structure (l'+dative + noun) is a Hebrew declaration of attribution: 'To X belongs Y.' See also Jonah 2:10 [9]: יְשׁוּעָתָה לַיהוָה ('Deliverance is YHWH's').
textual_notes: Psalm 3:9 [8]: לַיהוָה הַיְשׁוּעָה עַל עַמְּךָ בִרְכָתֶךָ סֶּלָה ('To YHWH belongs the salvation; upon your people your blessing. Selah.'). The Revelation text quotes the first clause and extends it to include the lamb as co-recipient of the declaration.

verses.translation: And all{H3605} the messengers{H4397} standing{H5975} around{H5439} the throne{H3678} and the elders{H2205} and the living-creatures{H2416}, and falling{H5307} upon their faces{H6440} before the throne{H3678}, and praying{H6419} to YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpallelim — 'praying', H6419, hitpael of פלל) — the definitive Hebrew word for prayer/intercession (Gen 20:7, 1 Sam 1:10, 1 Kings 8:30, Dan 9:4). Greek: προσεκύνησαν ('worshipped/prostrated'). These are fundamentally different acts — prayer vs. prostration. A back-translator from Greek would write הִשְׁתַּחֲווּ (hishtachavu — 'bowed down/worshipped'), the standard LXX equivalent of προσκυνέω, NOT the prayer verb mitpallelim.

Uses חַיּוֹת (chayyot — 'living-creatures', H2416) — Ezekiel's specific term for the throne-bearing creatures (Ezek 1:5,13-15,19-22; 3:13; 10:15,17,20). This is not a generic word for 'animals' but a technical Ezekiel term. Greek ζῷα ('living beings') is close but lacks the specific Ezekiel resonance.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'praying to YHWH' (prayer verb + Tetragrammaton). Greek: 'worshipped God' (prostration verb + generic divine title).
translation_notes: 'Praying' for mitpallelim — the hitpael of פלל is the standard Hebrew prayer verb, covering petition, intercession, and worship-through-speech. It implies verbal communion, not mere prostration.
'Living-creatures' for chayyot preserves the Ezekiel throne-vision connection without misleadingly rendering it as 'animals' or 'beasts.'

verses.translation: And saying{H559}: Praise{H7623} and thanksgiving{H3034} and praises{H8416} and glory{H3519} and splendor{H8597} and power{H3581} and might{H1369} shall be to our Elohim{H430}, [from eternity{H5769}] and unto{H5704} eternity{H5769}. Amen{H543}.

one_way_hebrew: The sevenfold doxology uses distinctly Hebrew liturgical vocabulary: שֶׁבַח (shebach — 'praise'), הוֹדָאָה (hoda'ah — 'thanksgiving'), תְּהִילּוֹת (tehillot — 'praises', the word that titles the Book of Psalms). Greek's sevenfold list differs significantly: εὐλογία (blessing), δόξα (glory), σοφία (WISDOM), εὐχαριστία (thanksgiving), τιμή (honor), δύναμις (power), ἰσχύς (strength). Where Hebrew has תְּהִילּוֹת ('praises'), Greek has σοφία ('wisdom') — completely unrelated concepts. A back-translator could not independently produce this Hebrew liturgical vocabulary from the Greek list.

Hebrew: [מֵעוֹלָם] וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from eternity and unto eternity') — a BIDIRECTIONAL eternal formula encompassing both past and future. Greek: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of ages') — future-directed only. The Hebrew echoes Psalm 90:2: מֵעוֹלָם עַד עוֹלָם אַתָּה אֵל ('From eternity to eternity, you are El'). A back-translator from the Greek future-only formula would write לְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים, not the bidirectional Psalm formula.
greek_deviations: Hebrew sevenfold list: praise (שֶׁבַח), thanksgiving (הוֹדָאָה), praises (תְּהִילּוֹת), glory (כָּבוֹד), splendor (תִּפְאֶרֶת), power (כֹּחַ), might (גְבוּרָה). Greek sevenfold list: blessing (εὐλογία), glory (δόξα), wisdom (σοφία), thanksgiving (εὐχαριστία), honor (τιμή), power (δύναμις), strength (ἰσχύς). Only partial overlap; 'praises' vs. 'wisdom' is an irreconcilable difference.
Greek places Amen both before and after the doxology. Hebrew has Amen only at the end.
translation_notes: The bracketed [מֵעוֹלָם] indicates an editorial restoration of a damaged or missing word in the manuscript — a textual-critical feature characteristic of Hebrew manuscript tradition, not back-translation.
תְּהִילּוֹת (tehillot) is the plural of תְּהִלָּה (tehillah, H8416), the word that names the Book of Psalms (סֵפֶר תְּהִלִּים). Its appearance in a doxology is natural Hebrew worship language.
textual_notes: Psalm 90:2: מֵעוֹלָם עַד עוֹלָם אַתָּה אֵל — 'From eternity to eternity, you are El.' The Hebrew doxology formula echoes this.

verses.translation: And one{H259} of the elders{H2205} answered{H6030} and said{H559} to me: Who{H4310} are these dressed{H3847} in white{H3836} garments{H4403}, and from what place{H4725} did they come{H935}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses מֵאֵיזֶה מָקוֹם (me-eizeh maqom — 'from which place', H4725) where Greek has simply πόθεν ('whence'). The Hebrew asks about the specific place of origin; the Greek asks a generic directional question. The phrase מֵאֵיזֶה מָקוֹם is a distinctly Mishnaic Hebrew construction that a back-translator from Greek's simple πόθεν would never produce.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from which place did they come?' (מֵאֵיזֶה מָקוֹם — asks about specific place). Greek: 'whence did they come?' (πόθεν — generic direction).
translation_notes: מֵאֵיזֶה (me-eizeh — 'from which') is a post-biblical Hebrew interrogative, characteristic of Mishnaic syntax.
וַיַּעַן (vayya'an — 'and he answered', H6030) uses the wayyiqtol narrative form, natural for Hebrew storytelling.

verses.translation: And I said{H559} to him: My lord{H113}, you know{H3045}. And he said{H559} to me: These are those who come{H935} through{H8432} much{H7235} distress, and they washed{H7364} their garments{H899} and refined{H2212} their garments{H899} in the blood{H1818} of the lamb{H7716}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses וְזִקְּקוּ (v'ziqqu — 'and they refined', H2212, piel of זקק) — a METALLURGICAL term meaning to purify metals by smelting (Mal 3:3, Ps 12:7 [6], Job 28:1). Greek: ἐλεύκαναν (eleukanan — 'they whitened/bleached') from λευκαίνω. A back-translator from Greek would use הִלְבִּינוּ (hilbinu — 'they whitened') from the root לבן. The Hebrew says the garments were REFINED as silver in a crucible; the Greek says they were BLEACHED white. These are entirely different metaphors — refiner's fire vs. laundry. The Hebrew connects to Malachi 3:2-3 where the coming messenger will 'sit as a refiner and purifier (מְזַקֵּק) of silver.'

Hebrew: מִתּוֹךְ הַרְבֵּה צַעַר ('from the midst of much distress'). Greek: ἐκ τῆς θλίψεως τῆς μεγάλης ('out of the great tribulation'). Hebrew מִתּוֹךְ (mitoch — 'from the midst/through the center of') implies passing THROUGH the heart of distress, not merely coming out of it. And הַרְבֵּה (harbeh — 'much') is quantitative while Greek μεγάλης ('great') is qualitative. The Hebrew צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'distress') is a less technical term than Greek θλῖψις ('tribulation'). A back-translator from the technical Greek would use הַצָּרָה הַגְּדוֹלָה (ha-tsarah ha-gedolah — 'the great tribulation') from צרה (H6869).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'refined' (וְזִקְּקוּ — metallurgical purification). Greek: 'whitened' (ἐλεύκαναν — bleaching). Different conceptual world.
Hebrew: 'from the midst of much distress' (quantitative, non-technical). Greek: 'out of the great tribulation' (qualitative, with definite article suggesting a specific event).
translation_notes: 'Refined' for ziqqu — the root זקק means to purify metals by smelting. The garments are purified not by bleaching but through the refiner's fire of the lamb's blood.
צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'distress/trouble') is a post-biblical Hebrew form without a standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Malachi 3:2-3: 'For he is like a refiner's fire and like launderers' soap. He shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver (מְזַקֵּק וּמְטַהֵר כֶּסֶף), and he shall purify the sons of Levi.' The same root זקק links the purification of the saints' garments to the Malachi refining prophecy.

verses.translation: And because of this, they are before{H6440} the throne{H3678} of YHWH{H3068}, and they minister{H8334} to him day{H3117} and night{H3915}; and the one who sits{H3427} upon the throne{H3678} — [his presence] shall dwell upon them.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses וְשֵׁרְתוּ (v'shertu — 'and they minister', H8334, from שרת) — the specific verb for priestly/Levitical SERVICE before YHWH: Aaron's priestly garments worn 'when he ministers' (בְּשָׁרְתוֹ, Ex 28:35,43); the Levites 'minister before the tabernacle' (Num 1:50, 3:6); 'YHWH set apart Levi to minister before him' (Deut 10:8); Samuel 'ministered before YHWH' (1 Sam 2:11). Greek λατρεύουσιν ('they serve/worship') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would use עָבְדוּ (avdu — 'they served'), the standard equivalent of λατρεύω in the LXX. The Hebrew sees this innumerable company performing PRIESTLY ministry.

The feminine verb תָּדוּר ('she shall dwell', from root דור — 'to dwell', cf. Ps 84:11, Isa 38:12) appears with the masculine subject 'the one who sits on the throne' (וְזֶה שֶׁיֹּשֵׁב). This gender mismatch implies an unstated feminine entity as the actual dwelling agent — almost certainly the שְׁכִינָה (Shekhinah, the divine indwelling presence), which is grammatically feminine in Hebrew. Greek σκηνώσει ('shall tabernacle') has no gender marking, so this theological depth is invisible in the Greek. No back-translator would introduce a feminine verb where a masculine subject is clear.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the throne of YHWH' (הַכִּסֵּא יַהְוֶה — with Tetragrammaton). Greek: 'the throne of God' (τοῦ θρόνου τοῦ θεοῦ).
Hebrew: תָּדוּר (feminine — 'she shall dwell', hinting at Shekhinah). Greek: σκηνώσει ('shall tabernacle/tent') — genderless, with tabernacle connotation absent from Hebrew דור.
Hebrew uses 'in his temple' (ἐν τῷ ναῷ αὐτοῦ) is absent — the phrase appears only in Greek, not in this Hebrew text.
translation_notes: 'Minister' for shertu preserves the priestly-service connotation. This is the verb of Levitical service before YHWH, not generic worship.
בִּשְׁבִיל (bishvil — 'because of/for the sake of') is a distinctly Mishnaic Hebrew preposition, absent from biblical Hebrew.

תָּדוּר from root דור ('to dwell', cf. Ps 84:11 מִדּוּר 'from dwelling') rather than the expected שכן ('to dwell/tabernacle') which would directly match the Greek σκηνόω. The choice of דור over שכן may be deliberate — avoiding the tabernacle-specific terminology.
textual_notes: 1 Chronicles 29:23: 'Solomon sat on the throne of YHWH (כִּסֵּא יְהוָה) as king.' The phrase 'throne of YHWH' is a specific OT construction.

verses.translation: They shall not hunger{H7456} and not thirst{H6770}, and scorching heat{H8273} and sun{H8121} shall not strike{H5221} them.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: This is a VERBATIM QUOTE from Isaiah 49:10: לֹא יִרְעָבוּ וְלֹא יִצְמָאוּ וְלֹא יַכֵּם שָׁרָב וָשָׁמֶשׁ — 'They shall not hunger and not thirst, and scorching heat and sun shall not strike them.' The Hebrew matches Isaiah WORD FOR WORD. Greek changes the order: ὁ ἥλιος (sun) first, then καῦμα (heat) — the reverse of Isaiah's and Hebrew Revelation's שָׁרָב (scorching heat) THEN שָׁמֶשׁ (sun). Greek also adds ἔτι ('anymore') twice, absent from both Isaiah and this Hebrew text. A back-translator from Greek would follow the Greek order and include ἔτι. The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's exact sequence.

Uses שָׁרָב (sharav, H8273 — 'scorching heat/mirage') — an extremely rare word occurring only in Isaiah 35:7 and 49:10 in the entire OT. Greek καῦμα ('heat') is a common, generic word. A back-translator would use the common חֹם (chom — 'heat', H2527), not the rare Isaiah-specific sharav. The presence of this rare vocabulary IS the Isaiah quotation — it could not arise independently.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'scorching heat and sun' (שָׁרָב וָשָׁמֶשׁ — Isaiah 49:10 order). Greek: 'the sun... any heat' (ὁ ἥλιος... πᾶν καῦμα — reversed order).
Greek adds ἔτι ('anymore') twice — absent from both the Hebrew and from Isaiah's original.
translation_notes: The pronoun וְהִיא (v'hi — feminine singular) preceding masculine plural verbs is notable. It likely functions as a collective pronoun referring back to the חַבְרוּתָה (fellowship, feminine noun) of v9, or as a discourse marker. The feminine reference preserves grammatical agreement with the feminine noun introduced four verses earlier.
textual_notes: Isaiah 49:10 (source text): לֹא יִרְעָבוּ וְלֹא יִצְמָאוּ וְלֹא יַכֵּם שָׁרָב וָשָׁמֶשׁ כִּי מְרַחֲמָם יְנַהֲגֵם וְעַל מַבּוּעֵי מַיִם יְנַהֲלֵם ('They shall not hunger nor thirst, scorching heat and sun shall not strike them, for he who has compassion on them shall lead them, and by springs of water shall guide them.'). The first half is quoted verbatim in v16; the second half's theme (leading to waters) is taken up in v17.

verses.translation: For the lamb{H7716} shall lead{H5090} them to a well{H875} of waters{H4325}, and YHWH{H3068} Elohim{H430} shall wipe{H4229} a tear{H1832} from upon all{H3605} faces{H6440}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בְּאֵר מַיִם (be'er mayim — 'a well of waters', H875). Greek: ζωσὰς πηγὰς ὑδάτων ('living springs of waters'). A back-translator from Greek πηγή ('spring/fountain') would write מַעְיָן (ma'yan — 'spring') or מָקוֹר (maqor — 'source/fountain'), NEVER בְּאֵר (be'er — 'well'). A well is DUG; a spring flows naturally. The Hebrew evokes the patriarchal wells of Genesis: Hagar's well (Gen 16:14), Be'er-sheva (Gen 21:31), Isaac's wells (Gen 26:18-25), the well where Jacob meets Rachel (Gen 29:2). Greek adds ζωσάς ('living') which is absent from Hebrew — the Hebrew's 'well of waters' is sufficient without the qualifier.

CRITICAL: The second half is a NEAR-VERBATIM QUOTE from Isaiah 25:8: וּמָחָה אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה דִּמְעָה מֵעַל כָּל פָּנִים ('And the Lord YHWH will wipe a tear from upon all faces'). This Hebrew text has יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים instead of אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה, but the construction is identical: 'shall wipe... a tear... from upon all faces' (מָחָה...דִּמְעָה...מֵעַל כָּל פָּנִים). Greek: ἐξαλείψει ὁ θεὸς πᾶν δάκρυον ἐκ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν ('God shall wipe every tear from their eyes'). The Greek changes 'from upon all FACES' to 'from their EYES,' and 'a tear' to 'every tear.' A back-translator from Greek would write כָּל דִּמְעָה מֵעֵינֵיהֶם, not the Isaiah quotation.

Uses יְנַהֲגֵם (yenahaagem — 'shall lead them', H5090) — continuing the Isaiah 49:10 allusion where the second half reads כִּי מְרַחֲמָם יְנַהֲגֵם ('for he who has compassion on them shall LEAD them'). The SAME verb נהג in the SAME conjugation. The lamb takes the role of Isaiah's 'compassionate one.' Greek uses TWO verbs: ποιμανεῖ ('shall shepherd') AND ὁδηγήσει ('shall guide'). A back-translator from Greek would produce both verbs, not the single נהג that directly quotes Isaiah.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a well of waters' (בְּאֵר מַיִם — dug well, no modifier). Greek: 'living springs of waters' (ζωσὰς πηγὰς ὑδάτων — natural springs, with 'living' modifier). Different water source entirely.

Hebrew: 'a tear from upon all faces' (דִּמְעָה מֵעַל כָּל פָּנִים — Isaiah 25:8 quotation). Greek: 'every tear from their eyes' (πᾶν δάκρυον ἐκ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν). Different body part (faces vs. eyes), different quantity (a tear vs. every tear).
Hebrew: one verb 'shall lead them' (יְנַהֲגֵם — from Isaiah 49:10). Greek: two verbs 'shall shepherd... and shall guide' (ποιμανεῖ... ὁδηγήσει). Greek adds the shepherding verb.
Greek adds 'that which is in the midst of the throne' (τὸ ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ θρόνου) — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Well of waters' for be'er mayim — preserving the dug-well imagery that evokes the patriarchal narrative. A well requires labor and intention; it is sought and found.
'Shall lead' for yenahaagem — the verb נהג (H5090) means to drive/lead, used for driving flocks (Gen 31:18, Ex 3:1) and leading people (Isa 49:10, 2 Chr 25:11).
textual_notes: Isaiah 49:10b: כִּי מְרַחֲמָם יְנַהֲגֵם וְעַל מַבּוּעֵי מַיִם יְנַהֲלֵם ('for he who has compassion on them shall lead them, and by springs of water shall guide them'). The Revelation Hebrew substitutes בְּאֵר (well) for מַבּוּעֵי (springs) but preserves the verb נהג and the leading-to-waters theme. The lamb takes the role of Isaiah's 'compassionate one' (מְרַחֲמָם).

Isaiah 25:8: וּמָחָה אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה דִּמְעָה מֵעַל כָּל פָּנִים — the identical construction appears here with a different divine name form (YHWH Elohim instead of Adonai YHVH). This is the same Isaiah 25:8 quotation found in Revelation 21:4.

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 7 in Hebrew contains some of the most decisive one-way translation markers in the entire book. The chapter quotes Isaiah 49:10 VERBATIM in v16, preserving the exact word order, the rare vocabulary שָׁרָב (sharav — appearing only in Isa 35:7 and 49:10), and the precise phrasing that the Greek rearranges and expands. It quotes Isaiah 25:8 in v17, preserving 'from upon all faces' (מֵעַל כָּל פָּנִים) where the Greek shifts to 'from their eyes.' The Ezekiel 9:4 תָּו (tav-mark) in v3 is among the strongest one-way markers in all of Revelation — the Hebrew uses the specific prophetic term for the forehead-mark rather than the generic 'sealing' of the Greek. The Psalm 3:9 quotation in v10 (לְיַהְוֶה הַיְשׁוּעָה) is a concise Psalm formula that the Greek expands into a full descriptive clause. The Aramaic חַבְרוּתָה (chavruta — 'fellowship', v9), the Daniel 6:27 paired expression חַי וְקִיֵּים (v2), the priestly-service verb שֵׁרְתוּ (v15), the metallurgical verb זִקְּקוּ ('refined', v14), the generic עֲנָפִים ('branches', v9 — pointing to a Sukkot setting), the distinction between מִשְׁפְּחוֹת (clans, v4) and שֵׁבֶט (tribe, vv5-8), and the feminine verb תָּדוּר (v15 — implying the Shekhinah) all demonstrate Hebrew concepts that could not derive from the Greek text. Multiple Mishnaic Hebrew forms (בִשְׁבִיל, לְהַזִּיק, מֵאֵיזֶה, שׁוּם, חַבְרוּתָה, אֵילּוּ) coexist with biblical Hebrew and Aramaic, consistent with a text composed in the late Second Temple period. The Sukkot imagery of v9 (branches, Psalm-quoting cry of deliverance, standing before the throne) connects to Zechariah 14:16's prophecy that all nations will celebrate Sukkot in the age to come.
